source_text: Hoc enim ipsum quam insanum est, quod dicitis, primo dolorem pariendi comitem esse peccati, cum ita perspicue ad sexuum conditionem magis, quam ad criminum respiciat ultionem, ut omnia animalia nullo maculata peccato, hos angores, hos gemitus in parturitione patiantur? Per quod apparet, argumentum non esse peccati, quod inveniri etiam sine peccato potest. Deinde promoventes affertis aliud, multo ineptissimum. Non doleret, inquis, femina, nisi esset criminum particeps. Verum illico subditis: Sed hoc peccatum, propter quod dolet mulier, non in pariente, ceterum in nascente deprehenditur. Nam ideo et baptizatae mulieres, liberae, ais, agitant a peccato; sed pro filiorum iniquitate, quos edunt, fecunditatis suae difficultatibus affliguntur. Qua opinione tradux peccati non iam a matre decurrit in sobolem, sed in parentes a nascente refunditur. Nam si ideo mulier baptizata sentit dolores, quia iniquitates inveniuntur in parvulo; supina incipit tradux esse, non prona. At non ideo cruciatur, quia iniquitatem filius habet; sed ideo quia eam secum ipsa, cum nasceretur, advexerat. Verum hoc malum sublatum ab ea per gratiam dixeras; si ergo peccato dolor parturientis adhaerebat, amotio peccati cruciatui parturitionum debuit mederi. Aut si cruciatus hic sine iniquitate esse non potest, qui tamen post Baptisma in feminis invenitur; iniquitas quoque eis non est dempta per gratiam, et eviluit pompa Baptismatis. Si autem in his mysteriis ea quam nos credimus, non vos fingitis, fuit virtus et veritas, sublatumque est omne peccatum, remanet dolor tamen, qui partus difficultate generatur; manifestum est illum gemitum naturae indicem esse, non culpae; quem te quoque annuente patiuntur, quas a Manichaeorum peccato liberatas fateris. Porro id exemplis rerum solis apparuit; si vero inspiciamus et ipsius verba sententiae, nae illa vestras nebulas splendidiore fulgore solis radiis dissolvet. Non est quippe dictum ad mulierem: Orientur in te dolores, aut: Generabo tibi gemitus; ut post culpam sensus eorum institui viderentur; sed: Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo tristitias tuas. Ostendit iam esse in naturali ratione, quod se in peccatrice persona non condere, sed multiplicare promittit. Numquam quippe multiplicantur nisi exstantia; ceterum antequam sint, fieri quidem proprie, augeri autem praepropere nuncupantur. Denique, ne hoc nostrum magis, quam ipsius veritatis esse videatur, hic in cunctis animantibus verborum refertur ordo servatus. De homine quoque priusquam fieret: Faciamus, inquit Deus, hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram [n156] ; et denuo de muliere: Dixit, inquit, Deus: Non est bonum esse solum hominem; faciamus ei adiutorium simile sui [n157] . Postea vero, quam facti sunt: Benedixit eis, inquit, dicens: Crescite et multiplicamini, et implete terram. Antequam conderentur, non est dictum: Multiplicentur; sed: Fiat homo; posteaquam exstitit qui acciperet incrementa, consequenter adiungit: Crescite et multiplicamini, et implete terram [n158] . Hoc itaque ordine gemitus parturitionum, qui secundum naturam fuerat, ita in hominum corporibus, sicut in pecoribus institutus, non conditur in Eva, sed crescit, ut peculiari granditate excitatorum affligeretur angorum. Nec tamen ad posterae aetatis feminas, nisi naturali mediocritate et corporum varietate pertingerent. Ibi ergo, non ut doleret in pariendo mulier, de peccato fuit, sed ut nimis doleret; sicut etiam temporibus diversis debilitates corporum pro peccatis, quibusdam legimus accidisse; sed non illa ampliatio miseriarum parcimoniam modi naturalis evertit. Nec tamen omnia quae in eadem sententia continentur, animadvertentis vigore clauduntur. Ceterum quaedam ibi pars indicat meritum, quaedam designat officium. Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo tristitias tuas et gemitum tuum; in tristitia paries filios. Huc usque ultio, quam non natura, sed persona promeruit. Iam hinc simpliciter posterioris sexus munus ostenditur: Ad virum, inquit, tuum conversio tua, et ipse tui dominabitur. Hoc nimirum non spectat ad poenam, quod nisi esset, spectaret ad culpam; ut viro quippe mulier modesto subdatur affectu, ordo est, supplicium non est. Caput enim, secundum Apostolum, mulieris, vir [n159] ; quia non est creatus homo propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum [n160] . Si ergo caput suum congruo pudore veneretur, naturae instituta custodit, non peccati tormenta perpetitur; cui ordini si resultaverit, rea est. Non est ergo in miseria functio rei, cuius neglectus in noxa est.
pass_a_gloss: For how insane is this itself which you say, first that the pain of giving birth is a companion of sin, when it so clearly looks to the condition of the sexes more than to a vengeance of charges, that all animals stained by no sin suffer these anguishes, these groans in parturition? Through which it appears that that is not an argument of sin, which can be found even without sin. Then promoting you bring another, much most inept. A female would not grieve, you say, unless she were a participant of charges. But immediately you subjoin: But this sin, on account of which a woman grieves, is caught not in the one giving birth, but in the one being born. For therefore even baptized women, free, you say, agitate from sin; but for the iniquity of sons whom they bring forth, they are afflicted by the difficulties of their fertility. By which opinion the tradux of sin no longer runs down from the mother into offspring, but is poured back into parents from the one being born. For if therefore a baptized woman feels pains, because iniquities are found in a little one; the tradux begins to be supine, not prone. But she is not therefore tormented because the son has iniquity; but therefore because she herself, when she was born, had brought it with her. But you had said this evil was taken away from her through grace; if therefore the pain of the one giving birth was clinging to sin, the removal of sin ought to have healed the torment of parturitions. Or if this torment cannot be without iniquity, which nevertheless is found after Baptism in females; iniquity also was not taken from them through grace, and the pomp of Baptism has grown cheap. But if in these mysteries there was that virtue and truth which we believe, not which you feign, and every sin was taken away, pain nevertheless remains, which is generated by the difficulty of birth; it is manifest that that groan is an index of nature, not of fault; which with you also granting those suffer, whom you confess freed from the sin of the Manichaeans. Further it appeared by examples of things alone; but if we inspect also the words of the sentence itself, truly it will dissolve your clouds by a more splendid brightness of the sun's rays. For it was not said to the woman: Pains will arise in you, or: I will generate groans for you; so that after fault the sense of them would seem to be instituted; but: Multiplying, he says, I will multiply your sadnesses. He showed there already is in the natural reason, what he promises not to found in a sinning person, but to multiply. For never are things multiplied except existing; for the rest before they are, they are named indeed properly to be made, but too hastily to be increased. Finally, lest this seem more ours than of truth itself, here in all living beings the order of words is reported kept. About the human also before he was made: Let us make, God says, a human to our image and likeness; and again about the woman: God said, it says: It is not good for the human to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself. But after they were made: He blessed them, it says, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth. Before they were founded, it was not said: Let them be multiplied; but: Let a human be made; after he existed who would receive increases, he consequently joins: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth. By this order therefore the groan of parturitions, which had been according to nature, so instituted in the bodies of humans as in cattle, is not founded in Eve, but grows, so that she would be afflicted by a peculiar greatness of stirred anguishes. Nor nevertheless would they reach the females of a later age, except by a natural mediocrity and a variety of bodies. There therefore, not that a woman would grieve in giving birth, was from sin, but that she would grieve too much; as also at diverse times we read weaknesses of bodies happened to certain people for sins; but that amplification of miseries does not overturn the sparingness of a natural measure. Nor nevertheless are all things which are contained in the same sentence closed by the vigor of one noticing. For the rest a certain part there indicates desert, a certain designates office. Multiplying, he says, I will multiply your sadnesses and your groan; in sadness you will bear sons. Thus far vengeance, which not nature but a person deserved. Already from here simply the gift of the later sex is shown: To your husband, he says, is your turning, and he will lord it over you. This indeed does not look to a penalty, which unless it were, would look to a fault; that a woman be subjected to a man by a modest affection is order, it is not a punishment. For the head, according to the Apostle, of the woman is the man; because the human was not created on account of the woman, but the woman on account of the man. If therefore she venerates her head with a fitting modesty, she keeps the institutions of nature, she does not endure the torments of sin; if she has rebounded against which order, she is guilty. There is therefore not in misery the function of a thing, whose neglect is in harm.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS parvulus; Blaise infants as Julian's test case

pass_b_english: First, how insane is your very claim that childbirth pain accompanies sin! It so plainly concerns the condition of the sexes rather than punishment for crimes that all animals, stained by no sin, undergo these pangs and groans in giving birth. This shows that something found even without sin is not proof of sin.

Then you advance another, far more foolish claim. ‘A woman would not suffer pain,’ you say, ‘unless she shared in crimes.’ Yet immediately you add: ‘But this sin, for which the woman suffers, is found not in the mother but in the child being born.’ (1 Corinthians 11:3) Thus, you say, even baptized women live free from sin, yet are afflicted by the difficulties of their childbearing because of the iniquity of the children they bring forth. On this opinion, inherited sin no longer flows from mother to offspring but pours back from the newborn into the parents. If a baptized woman feels pain because iniquities are found in the infant, transmission begins to run uphill rather than downhill.

‘But she is not tormented because her son has iniquity; rather, because she herself brought it with her when she was born.’ Yet you said grace removed this evil from her. If a laboring woman’s pain adhered to sin, removing sin should have cured childbirth’s torment. Or, if this torment cannot exist without iniquity, but is still found in women after baptism, then grace has not removed their iniquity either, and baptism’s ceremony has become worthless.

But if these mysteries possessed the power and truth we believe in, not what you invent, and every sin was removed, yet the pain caused by difficult childbirth remains, it is clear that this groaning indicates nature, not fault. Even you agree it is suffered by women whom you acknowledge freed from the Manichaeans’ sin. So much is clear from examples alone. If we inspect the words of the pronouncement itself, however, it will dissolve your fog with brilliance surpassing the sun’s rays.

The woman was not told, ‘Pains will arise within you,’ or, ‘I will create groaning for you,’ as though these sensations were instituted after her fault. Rather: ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows’ (Genesis 3:16). God shows that what he promises not to create but to multiply in the sinful person already exists in the natural order. Only existing things are multiplied. Before they exist, ‘making’ is the proper expression; calling it ‘increasing’ is premature.

Lest this seem our own point rather than truth’s, this same order of words is recorded concerning all living beings. Before humanity was made, God said: ‘Let us make humanity in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26). Again concerning the woman: ‘God said: It is not good for the human to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself’ (Genesis 2:18). After they were made, however: ‘He blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). Before their creation he did not say ‘Let them multiply,’ but ‘Let humanity be made.’ Once someone existed who could increase, he appropriately added, ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth.’

In this same order, childbirth’s groaning, established naturally in human bodies as in animals, was not created in Eve but increased, so that she would suffer a special intensity of heightened pangs. Yet these would reach later women only in the ordinary natural measure, varying with their bodies. Thus sin did not cause the woman to suffer in childbirth, but to suffer excessively. Similarly, we read of bodily infirmities coming upon particular people for sins at different times; but such increased misery did not overturn the smaller natural measure.

Not everything in this pronouncement, however, is confined to punitive severity. One part indicates desert, another specifies a duty. ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children.’ Up to this point comes punishment, earned by the person, not by nature. From here the task of the sex created second is simply described: ‘Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you’ (Genesis 3:16). This plainly does not concern punishment: its absence would concern fault. A woman’s submission to her husband with modest affection belongs to order, not punishment. According to the apostle, ‘the husband is the woman’s head’ (Ephesians 5:23), because ‘man was not created for woman, but woman for man’ (1 Corinthians 11:9). If she reveres her head with fitting modesty, she maintains nature’s arrangements rather than enduring sin’s torments. If she resists that order, she is guilty. Performing something whose neglect is a fault is therefore no misery.
